rows.note: In the ayah ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ means humankind, and Hebrew אנש denotes a human being, often emphasizing mortality.

rows.explanation: אֱנוֹשׁ is “man” in the question of why God is mindful of him.
אֱנוֹשׁ is a human being whom God returns to dust.
אֱנוֹשׁ is a human being whose days are like grass.
אֱנוֹשׁ is “man” in a question about God’s regard for him.
אֱנוֹשׁ is mortal man in a question about whether he can be just before God.
אֱנוֹשׁ is “man” in a question about why God pays him attention.
אֱנוֹשׁ is “man” in a question about whether he can be pure.
אֱנוֹשׁ is mortal man, described here as a worm.
בֶּן־אֱנוֹשׁ means a human being who will perish like grass.
The Aramaic phrase כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ means “like a son of man,” using the same human noun.

rows.note: In the ayah خُسْرٍ is humanity’s loss or ruin, while Hebrew חסר chiefly means lacking, falling short, or becoming diminished.

rows.explanation: וַיַּחְסְרוּ says the floodwaters diminished, a concrete decrease related to loss.
וַיַּחְסְרוּ again says the floodwaters diminished.
לֹא חָסַרְתָּ דָּבָר means Israel lacked nothing, expressing the opposite of a shortfall.
לֹא־תֶחְסַר כֹּל בָּהּ says nothing will be lacking in the land.
לֹא אֶחְסָר means “I shall not want,” expressing the opposite of lack.
לֹא־יַחְסְרוּ כָל־טוֹב says those who seek the Lord will lack no good thing.
בַּחֲסַר־לֵב describes fools as lacking understanding, a harmful deficiency.
תֶּחְסָר says the wicked person’s belly will lack food.
מַחְסוֹר means poverty or want, an adverse outcome close to material loss.
מַחְסוֹר means want, the outcome assigned to haste.
חֶסֶר means poverty that will overtake someone pursuing riches.
The Aramaic חַסִּיר means “wanting” in the judgment that the king has been weighed and found deficient.
